# Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling

###### Abstract

The reliability of large language models (LLMs) during test-time scaling
is often assessed with _external verifiers_ or _reward models_ that
distinguish correct reasoning from flawed logic. Prior work has studied
both outcome reward models (ORMs), which assess only the final answer,
and process reward models (PRMs), which score intermediate reasoning
steps. Although PRMs are often viewed as advantageous due to their
finer-grained supervision, much of the supporting evidence comes from
math-adjacent settings, and their relative benefits across broader
domains remain unclear. We present the first unified evaluation of four
reward model variants, discriminative ORM and PRM (dORM, dPRM) and
generative ORM and PRM (gORM, gPRM), across 14 diverse domains. Contrary
to conventional wisdom, we find that (i) dORM performs on par with dPRM,
(ii) gPRM is not competitive, and (iii) overall, gORM is the most
robust, yielding significant and consistent gains across every tested
domain. We attribute the worse performance of gPRM to the stepwise
scoring process, which inherits label noise from LLM-based automatic
labeling, leading to difficulties in evaluating long reasoning
trajectories, including those involving self-correcting reasoning. Both
our theoretical analysis and empirical observations indicate that
stepwise aggregation compounds errors as reasoning length increases.
These findings challenge the common assumption that fine-grained
supervision is always better and support generative outcome verification
for multi-domain deployment. Our
[code](https://github.com/db-Lee/Multi-RM) is publicly available to
facilitate future research in multi-domain settings.

Reviewed on OpenReview:
[https://openreview.net/forum?id=PgouBhL7IR](https://openreview.net/forum?id=PgouBhL7IR)

## 1 Introduction

Test-time scaling (TTS) enables large language models (LLMs) to generate
diverse, reliable solutions via chain-of-thought reasoning ([Wei et al.,
2022](#bib.bib51); [Kojima et al., 2022](#bib.bib28); [Yao et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib56); [Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib34), CoT;) and has
shown strong results on challenging reasoning tasks ([Yao et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib55); [Snell et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53)). A widely adopted TTS approach uses _external
verifiers_ that select the best among the candidates ([Snell et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45)). A common external verifier is the outcome reward
model (ORM), typically implemented as a discriminative classifier that
assigns a scalar _reward_ to a CoT ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib7);
[Uesato et al., 2022](#bib.bib46); [Yu et al., 2024](#bib.bib57)). ORMs
are trained only on outcome-level signals, providing a single label per
trajectory rather than feedback at individual reasoning steps. Recent
work has introduced process reward models ([Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31); [Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib48); [Setlur et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib62), PRMs;) that score
each step of a CoT and aggregate the scores into a trajectory-level
reward. Supervised with high-quality, carefully constructed process
labels, e.g., manual annotation ([Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)) or
Monte Carlo rollouts ([Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib48)), PRMs have been
shown to outperform ORMs as TTS verifiers.

Beyond discriminative verifiers, several studies have shown that the
generative ability of LLMs can improve CoT verification, such as
*LLM-as-a-judge* ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib47); [Liu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib32); [Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib63)). Based on this
idea, other works fine-tune LLMs to generate a verification rationale
for a CoT and compute the final reward from token probabilities ([Zhang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib59); [Khalifa et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Zhao
et al., 2025](#bib.bib61)). To obtain verification CoTs for training,
most previous work adopts _consensus-filtering_: (i) generate
verification CoTs, and (ii) retain the verification CoT if its parsed
verdict aligns with outcome or process labels. After training, these
generative verifiers have shown strong performance in math-adjacent
reasoning tasks, outperforming discriminative verifiers.

However, external verifiers for TTS have been studied primarily in
math-adjacent domains. This narrow scope limits the potential for LLM
deployment in high-stakes real-world applications, such as the
legal ([Guha et al., 2023](#bib.bib18); [Cui et al., 2023](#bib.bib9);
[Fei et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)) and medical ([Singhal et al.,
2023](#bib.bib43); [Kung et al., 2023](#bib.bib29); [Singhal et al.,
2025](#bib.bib44)) domains, where trustworthiness is paramount and
rigorous verification of LLM outputs is especially important. Recently,
[Zeng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib58) proposed multi-domain PRMs trained on
the graduate-level benchmark ([Wang et al., 2024c](#bib.bib50),
MMLU-Pro;), covering 14 diverse domains, and showed that multi-domain
training for PRMs significantly improves TTS performance across diverse
domains. However, the study is _limited_ to discriminative PRMs and the
broader potential of different verifier types (e.g., ORMs vs. PRMs,
discriminative vs. generative) in the multi-domain setting remains
_underexplored_.

![Refer to caption](2510.00492v3/aha_reward_models.png)

Figure 1: Evaluating CoTs using gORM and gPRM.

To this end, we present the first controlled multi-domain TTS evaluation
of four verifier variants, discriminative ORM and PRM (dORM, dPRM), and
generative ORM and PRM (gORM, gPRM), trained and evaluated under a
common protocol across 14 diverse domains. We review these variants in
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and, under controlled conditions, evaluate them on math ([Lightman
et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib62), PRM800K,
ProcessBench;), multi-domain ([Wang et al., 2024c](#bib.bib50),
MMLU-Pro;), and specialized-domain ([Rein et al., 2024](#bib.bib40);
[Jin et al., 2021](#bib.bib24); [Fan et al., 2026](#bib.bib13),
GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, LEXam;) in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").
In the math domain, trends across the four variants are consistent with
prior work ([Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib59); [Khalifa et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)). dPRM
outperforms dORM, and generative variants outperform discriminative
ones. In the multi-domain and specialized domain setting, however, we
observe contrasting results. dORM performs on par with dPRM, gPRM is not
competitive, and overall, gORM delivers consistent and significant gains
over the others.

In
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
we identify two factors underlying the weaker performance of gPRM.
First, on more difficult multi-domain problems, LLMs tend to produce
longer CoTs that PRMs struggle to evaluate. As illustrated
in [Fig. 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
stepwise aggregation in PRMs often fails to reward long CoTs that
recover from earlier errors ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib20), “aha”
moments;), because verification stops at the first mistake. In
[Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
we analyze how this stepwise aggregation compounds errors as the chain
length increases, and confirm this effect empirically. Second, label
noise is prevalent in multi-domain datasets. Given that step annotation
in specialized domains is costly, prior work such as [Zeng et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib58) depends on LLM-based auto-labeling, which can
introduce noise. In
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
using a simulated label-noise analysis in the math domain, we show that
dPRM is particularly sensitive to noisy step labels, whereas gORM
remains robust. Although gPRM is robust to label noise in the math
domain, it degrades in the multi-domain setting. We attribute this
degradation to a severe shift in the CoT-length distribution induced by
consensus filtering. Based on this analysis, we present practical
guidelines for selecting among the four variants and discuss limitations
and future work in
[Section 5](#S5 "5 Practical Guidelines, Limitations, and Future Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").

Our contributions and findings are summarized as follows:

- •
  We present the first controlled multi-domain TTS evaluation of four
  verifier variants (dORM, dPRM, gORM, and gPRM) trained and evaluated
  under a common protocol across 14 diverse domains.
- •
  Contrary to conventional wisdom established in math-adjacent settings,
  we observe that (i) dORM performs similarly to dPRM, (ii) gPRM is not
  competitive, and (iii) overall, gORM delivers consistent gains over
  the others.
- •
  To explain the empirical observations, we provide two
  perspectives: (i) a theoretical analysis, with empirical support,
  showing that _PRM risk increases with CoT length_, and (ii) evidence
  of _process label risk_ in the multi-domain setting with
  length-distribution shift induced by _consensus filtering_.

## 2 Background and Related Work

In this section, we review background and related work. We first
formalize notation and test-time scaling in
[Section 2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
and then discuss reward-model variants in
[Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
summarized in
[Fig. 2](#S2.F2 "In TTS with reward models. ‣ 2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").

### 2.1 Problem Formulation

#### Notation.

For a given question $`q`$ with the corresponding ground-truth (GT)
answer $`a`$, we leverage the reasoning ability of LLMs to predict $`a`$
by generating a CoT, i.e.,
$`r_{1:T}\coloneqq(r_{1}\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}\ldots\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}r_{T})\sim p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(\cdot\mid q)`$.
Following [Zeng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib58), we segment the reasoning
steps $`r_{1:T}`$ using the delimiter “\n\n”, where $`T`$ is the number
of reasoning steps. Let
$`x\coloneqq(q\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}r_{1:T})\in\mathcal{X}`$,
where $`\mathcal{X}`$ denotes the space of questions and reasoning
chains, and let
$`x_{1:t}\coloneqq(q\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}r_{1:t})`$ be the prefix
up to the $`t`$-th step. We consider two types of labels: (1) the
_outcome label_
$`y=\mathbbm{1}(\hat{a}(r_{T})=a)\in\{0\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}1\}`$,
where $`\hat{a}(r_{T})`$ is the predicted answer retrieved from the last
reasoning step $`r_{T}`$ and $`\mathbbm{1}`$ is the indicator function;
and (2) the _process labels_
$`z_{1:T}=(z_{1}\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}\ldots\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}z_{T})\in\{0\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}1\}^{T}`$,
where each $`z_{t}`$ indicates whether the corresponding reasoning step
$`r_{t}`$ is correct. Note that $`y`$ represents the correctness label
for the last reasoning step, so $`y=z_{T}`$. We use $`y`$ (and
$`z_{t}`$) to denote both the label and the corresponding random
variable, where the event $`y=1`$ corresponds to the model generating
the positive verdict token (e.g., “Yes”). Thus, expressions such as
$`p(y=1\mid x)`$ denote the predicted probability of this event and are
well-defined at test time without access to the true label.

#### TTS with reward models.

Reward models have many applications, including LLM training via
reinforcement learning ([Ziegler et al., 2019](#bib.bib65); [Ouyang
et al., 2022](#bib.bib36); [Achiam et al., 2023](#bib.bib1); [Dubey
et al., 2024](#bib.bib12); [Gemma Team et al., 2024](#bib.bib16); [Yang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)), preference labeling ([Dong et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11); [Meng et al., 2024](#bib.bib35); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2)), rejection sampling ([Gulcehre et al.,
2023](#bib.bib19); [Dong et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)), and data
filtering ([Dubey et al., 2024](#bib.bib12); [Albalak et al.,
2024](#bib.bib3); [Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)). In this work, we
focus on parallel or sampling-based ([Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)) TTS
with reward models, such as Best-of-$`N`$ ([Charniak & Johnson,
2005](#bib.bib6); [Khalifa et al., 2023](#bib.bib26); [Snell et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45), Bo$`N`$;), which allocates more compute at test time
(i.e., generates $`N`$ CoTs) and selects the candidate
$`\hat{a}(r^{(i_{\star})}_{T})`$ with the highest _reward_:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
i_{\star}=\argmax_{i\in\{1\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}\ldots\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}N\}}f(x^{(i)})\mathchar 59\relax\quad\text{where }x^{(i)}\coloneqq(q\mathchar 59\relax r_{1:T}^{(i)})\mathchar 59\relax\;\text{and }\;r_{1:T}^{(i)}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}p_{\mathtt{LLM}}(\cdot\mid q).
``` |  | (1) |

Here, $`f:\mathcal{X}\to[0\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}1]`$ is the *true
(unknown) reward function* that assigns higher scores to CoTs that yield
more reasonable and correct answers. However, $`f`$ is unknown, so we
train an *external verifier*
$`\hat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to[0\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}1]`$ to
approximate $`f`$ and use $`\hat{f}`$ as a surrogate in
[Eq. 1](#S2.E1 "In TTS with reward models. ‣ 2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
which is detailed in
[Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").

![Refer to caption](2510.00492v3/reward_models.png)

Figure 2: Conceptual illustration of reward models: $`r_{2}`$ is the
first incorrect step; the final answer is correct.

### 2.2 Reward Models

#### Discriminative outcome reward model (dORM).

Early studies on reward models ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib7); [Uesato
et al., 2022](#bib.bib46); [Yu et al., 2024](#bib.bib57)) train a binary
classifier
$`\hat{f}_{\textsf{dORM}}:\mathcal{X}\mapsto[0\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}1]`$
on *outcome labels $`y\in\{0\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}1\}`$ only*,
without requiring the intermediate process labels
$`(z_{1}\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}\ldots\mathchar 59\relax z_{T-1})`$.
Specifically, they sample CoTs and answers for given questions,
construct a training dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{dORM}}\coloneqq\{(x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}y)\}`$,
and train $`\hat{f}_{\textsf{dORM}}`$ with the binary cross-entropy
(BCE) loss to approximate true $`p(y=1\mid x)`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\textsf{dORM}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{dORM}}|}\sum_{(x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}y)\in\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{dORM}}}\ell_{\mathtt{BCE}}\left(\hat{f}_{\textsf{dORM}}(x)\mathchar 59\relax y\right)\mathchar 59\relax
``` |  | (2) |

with
$`\ell_{\mathtt{BCE}}(x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}y)=-\bigl[y\log x+(1-y)\log(1-x)\bigr]`$.
It is important to note that while dORM takes the full chain-of-thought
as input and can leverage intermediate reasoning to predict final
correctness, its fundamental characteristic is *outcome-level
supervision and global scoring*. Despite this coarser supervision,
[Uesato et al. (2022)](#bib.bib46) demonstrated that outcome-based
feedback achieves comparable final-answer accuracy to process
supervision when training the generator LLM $`p_{\mathtt{LLM}}`$. While
their focus is on policy training rather than external test-time
verification, their finding highlights the strong baseline efficacy of
outcome signals.

#### Discriminative process reward model (dPRM).

dPRM seeks to improve the reward signal by training on fine-grained
feedback for intermediate reasoning steps, i.e., *process labels*
$`z_{1:T}`$. For dPRM, the quality of these labels is the primary
factor. Accordingly, prior work has proposed collecting process labels
for sampled CoTs via manual annotation ([Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31)), Monte Carlo (MC) rollouts ([Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib48)), automatically generated labels from LLMs ([Zeng
et al., 2025](#bib.bib58)), or combinations thereof ([Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib60)). After collecting the process labels, we construct
the training set
$`\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{dPRM}}\coloneqq\{(x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}z_{1:T})\}`$
and train $`\hat{f}_{\textsf{dPRM}}`$ using the BCE loss at each step:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\textsf{dPRM}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{dPRM}}|}\sum_{(x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}z_{1:T})\in\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{dPRM}}}\frac{1}{{T}^{\prime}}\sum_{t=1}^{{T}^{\prime}}\ell_{\mathtt{BCE}}\left(\hat{f}_{\textsf{dPRM}}(x_{1:t})\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}z_{t}\right)\mathchar 59\relax
``` |  | (3) |

where $`{T}^{\prime}`$ is the index of the first incorrect reasoning
step, i.e.,
$`{T}^{\prime}\coloneqq\min(\{t\in\{1\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}\dots\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}T\}:z_{t}=0\}\cup\{T\})`$.
Training up to the $`{T}^{\prime}`$-th step reflects a common assumption
in the literature ([Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib48); [Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Zeng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib58)): once a reasoning step is incorrect, *subsequent
steps are also incorrect*, i.e., if $`z_{t}=0`$ then
$`z_{t^{\prime}}=0`$ for all
$`t^{\prime}\in\{t+1\mathchar 59\relax\ldots\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}T\}`$.
At test time, we approximate $`f`$ in
[Eq. 1](#S2.E1 "In TTS with reward models. ‣ 2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
by aggregating the step rewards with the *minimum*¹¹ 1
[Tables 8](#A7.T8 "In Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[9](#A7.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[10](#A7.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[11](#A7.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [12](#A7.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
show that minimum, average, product, and last-step aggregation yield
only marginal differences, with minimum aggregation slightly
outperforming the others overall, consistent with [Zeng et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib58). ([Zeng et al., 2025](#bib.bib58)). Thus, in
contrast to the global scoring of ORMs, the defining characteristic of
PRMs is *process-level supervision and step-score aggregation*.

#### LLM-as-a-judge.

[Wang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib47); [Liu et al. (2023)](#bib.bib32);
[Zheng et al. (2023)](#bib.bib63) show that the task-generalization
ability of LLMs can extend to verification (i.e., zero-shot CoT
verification). However, LLMs often “overthink” ([Bavaresco et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5)) and, without additional training, remain practically
limited ([Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)), implying the need for LLMs
explicitly trained for verification.

#### Generative outcome reward model (gORM).

[Zhang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib59) proposed gORM, trained to generate a
*verification CoT* together with a binary verdict, e.g., “Verification:
Is the answer correct? Yes” or “No”. Because GT verification CoTs are
unavailable, they synthesize training data via a consensus-filtering
mechanism ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib49); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64)). We first sample a verification CoT and verdict from
an LLM-as-a-judge, i.e.,
$`v_{1:L}\sim p_{\mathtt{LLM\text{-}j}}(\cdot\mid x)`$ using the prompt
format in
[Fig. 18](#A2.F18 "In Appendix B Prompts ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").
Here, $`v_{1:L}\in\mathcal{V}^{L}`$ denotes the verification-CoT token
sequence (including the verdict tokens), $`\mathcal{V}`$ is the
vocabulary, and let $`\hat{y}\in\{0\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}1\}`$ be
the parsed verdict ($`1`$ for “Yes”, $`0`$ for “No”). We then include
$`(x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:L})`$ in the training set
$`\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{gORM}}`$ only if $`\hat{y}`$ agrees with the
known outcome label $`y`$. We train $`p_{\textsf{gORM}}`$ with the
next-token prediction over verification CoTs $`v_{1:L}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\textsf{gORM}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{gORM}}|}\sum_{(x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}v_{1:L})\in\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{gORM}}}\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}-\log p_{\textsf{gORM}}(v_{i}\mid x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}v_{<i}).
``` |  | (4) |

$`-\log p_{\textsf{gORM}}`$ is implemented as the cross-entropy loss
over $`\mathcal{V}`$. At test time, we approximate $`f`$ with:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{f}_{\textsf{gORM}}(x)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{v_{1:L}\sim p_{\textsf{gORM}}(\cdot\mid x)}\!\bigl[p_{\textsf{gORM}}(y=1\mid x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}v_{1:L})\bigr]\;\approx\;\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}p_{\textsf{gORM}}\left(y=1\mid x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}v_{1:L}^{(i)}\right)\mathchar 59\relax
``` |  | (5) |

where
$`v_{1:L}^{(i)}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}p_{\textsf{gORM}}(\cdot\mid x)`$.
Here, the expectation is approximated with $`M`$ MC samples and the
model’s normalized probability of predicting the verdict “Yes” at the
last verdict position:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\textsf{gORM}}(y=1\mid v_{1:L}\mathchar 59\relax x)\coloneqq\dfrac{p_{\textsf{gORM}}(\text{``{Yes}''}\mid x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:(L-1)})}{p_{\textsf{gORM}}(\text{``{Yes}''}\mid x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:(L-1)})+p_{\textsf{gORM}}(\text{``{No}''}\mid x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:(L-1)})}.
``` |  | (6) |

#### Generative Process Reward Model (gPRM).

Beyond gORM, [Khalifa et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27) proposed gPRM, which is
trained to generate verification CoTs $`v_{1:L}`$ with *stepwise process
verdicts*, e.g., “Step t: The step is \boxed{correct}” or
“\boxed{incorrect}”. Let the predicted verdict sequence be
$`\hat{z}_{1:{T}^{\prime}}\in\{0\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}1\}^{{T}^{\prime}}`$,
defined up to the first predicted incorrect step $`{T}^{\prime}`$²² 2 As
shown in
[Fig. 19](#A2.F19 "In Appendix B Prompts ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
when generating verification CoTs for gPRM (i.e.,
$`v_{1:L}\sim p_{\mathtt{LLM\text{-}j}}(\cdot\mid x)`$), [Khalifa et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib27) instruct the LLM-as-a-judge
$`p_{\mathtt{LLM\text{-}j}}`$ to stop once it detects the first
incorrect step. . Following [Khalifa et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27), we
append a final verdict prompt, yielding the token sequence
$`v_{1:L^{+}}`$ by concatenating “Is the solution correct? Yes” if all
predicted process labels are $`1`$
($`\hat{z}_{1:{T}^{\prime}}=\mathbf{1}_{{T}^{\prime}}`$), and “No”
otherwise. We then construct
$`\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{gPRM}}\coloneqq\{(x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:L^{+}})\}`$
only when the predicted prefix agrees with the GT
($`\hat{z}_{1:{T}^{\prime}}=z_{1:{T}^{\prime}}`$). We train
$`p_{\textsf{gPRM}}`$ with $`v_{1:L^{+}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\textsf{gPRM}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{gPRM}}|}\sum_{(x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}v_{1:L^{+}})\in\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{gPRM}}}\frac{1}{L^{+}}\sum_{i=1}^{L^{+}}-\log p_{\textsf{gPRM}}(v_{i}\mid x_{1:{T}^{\prime}}\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}v_{<i}).
``` |  | (7) |

We condition on $`x_{1:T^{\prime}}`$ rather than the full input $`x`$
for training ([Khalifa et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)), since the model
$`p_{\textsf{gPRM}}`$ is prompted to stop verification once it reaches
the first incorrect step, analogous to the data-generation process
([Fig. 20](#A2.F20 "In Appendix B Prompts ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).
At test time, consistent with
[Eqs. 5](#S2.E5 "In Generative outcome reward model (gORM). ‣ 2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [6](#S2.E6 "Eq. 6 ‣ Generative outcome reward model (gORM). ‣ 2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
we approximate $`f`$ in
[Eq. 1](#S2.E1 "In TTS with reward models. ‣ 2.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
by sampling from $`p_{\textsf{gPRM}}`$ and computing the normalized
probability of a positive final verdict:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{f}_{\textsf{gPRM}}(x)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{v_{1:L^{+}}\sim p_{\textsf{gPRM}}(\cdot\mid x)}\!\left[p_{\textsf{gPRM}}(y=1\mid x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}v_{1:L^{+}})\right]\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}p_{\textsf{gPRM}}\left(y=1\mid x\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}v_{1:L^{+}}^{(i)}\right)\mathchar 59\relax
``` |  | (8) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\textsf{gPRM}}(y=1\mid x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:L^{+}})\coloneqq\dfrac{p_{\textsf{gPRM}}(\text{``{Yes}''}\mid x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:(L^{+}-1)})}{p_{\textsf{gPRM}}(\text{``{Yes}''}\mid x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:(L^{+}-1)})+p_{\textsf{gPRM}}(\text{``{No}''}\mid x\mathchar 59\relax v_{1:(L^{+}-1)})}\mathchar 59\relax
``` |  | (9) |

where
$`v_{1:L^{+}}^{(i)}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}p_{\textsf{gPRM}}(\cdot\mid x)`$
and we now condition on the full input $`x`$ at test time ([Khalifa
et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)). Recent work has proposed more advanced gPRM
architectures to improve generalization and mitigate evaluation
artifacts, such as incorporating code verification ([Zhao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib61)) or reasoning-driven generative evaluations ([She
et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)). However, these methods are primarily
optimized for the math domain and do not directly extend to multi-domain
data (e.g., legal or medical domains). Therefore, we follow the approach
of [Khalifa et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27) in this work.

## 3 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate dORM, dPRM, gORM, and gPRM in the math
domain and the multi-domain setting. We describe experimental setups
([Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
and present results
([Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).

### 3.1 Experimental Setups

#### Math datasets.

For the math domain, we use PRM800K ([Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31)) for training, where the process labels $`z_{1:T}`$
are human-annotated. As a testbed, we use
[ProcessBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Qwen/ProcessBench) ([Zheng
et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)) with four splits: GSM8K, Math, Omni-Math, and
OlympiadBench. We generate $`N{=}16`$ CoTs per question in GSM8K and
Math with
[Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) ([Qwen
Team, 2024a](#bib.bib37)) for TTS; since we only seek to verify that a
controlled evaluation reproduces prior findings, we restrict TTS to this
setting.

#### Multi-domain and specialized-domain datasets.

Following [Zeng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib58), we primarily use
MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024c](#bib.bib50)), a 10-choice benchmark
covering 14 domains. Each question is paired with 16 CoTs for training
and 128 for evaluation, generated by
[Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) ([Dubey
et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)), where process labels $`z_{1:T}`$ are
*automatically annotated* by
[Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct).
To assess generalization across different $`p_{\mathtt{LLM}}`$, we
generate $`N{=}16`$ CoTs per question using
[SmolLM3-3B](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B) ([Bakouch
et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)),
[Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct),
[gemma-2-9b-it](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-2-9b-it) ([Gemma
Team et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)), and
[Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct).
For broader assessment, we also include additional specialized-domain
benchmarks: the graduate-level science benchmark ([Rein et al.,
2024](#bib.bib40), GPQA-Diamond;), the medical benchmark ([Jin et al.,
2021](#bib.bib24), MedQA;), and the legal benchmark ([Fan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13), LEXam;).

#### Implementation details.

For the reward-model backbones, we use the [R1-Distill
models](https://huggingface.co/collections/deepseek-ai/deepseek-r1-678e1e131c0169c0bc89728d) ([Guo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)):
[Qwen-1.5B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B)
and
[Qwen-7B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B)
for the math domain, and
[Llama-8B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B)
and
[Qwen-14B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B)
for the multi-domain setting, respectively. We also use
[Qwen3-8B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B) as the backbone to
assess whether the results hold for non-distilled backbones in the
multi-domain setting. We follow [Zhang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib59) for
the gORM prompt template
([Fig. 18](#A2.F18 "In Appendix B Prompts ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"))
and [Khalifa et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27) for gPRM
([Fig. 20](#A2.F20 "In Appendix B Prompts ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).
We optimize reward models using AdamW ([Loshchilov & Hutter,
2019](#bib.bib33)) with LoRA ([Hu et al., 2022](#bib.bib23)). For gORM
and gPRM, we sample $`M=16`$ verification CoTs in the math setting and
$`M=10`$ in the multi-domain setting (cf.
[Eqs. 5](#S2.E5 "In Generative outcome reward model (gORM). ‣ 2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [8](#S2.E8 "Eq. 8 ‣ Generative Process Reward Model (gPRM). ‣ 2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
using [vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) ([Kwon et al.,
2023](#bib.bib30)). See
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[Table 2](#A4.T2 "In Backbones for reward models. ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [this repository](https://github.com/db-Lee/Multi-RM) for more
details.

#### Verification CoTs.

Following [Zhang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib59) and [Khalifa et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib27), we construct verification-CoT datasets for gORM and
gPRM by prompting [QwQ-32B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/QwQ-32B) ([Qwen
Team, 2025](#bib.bib39)) with the formats in
[Figs. 18](#A2.F18 "In Appendix B Prompts ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [19](#A2.F19 "Fig. 19 ‣ Appendix B Prompts ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").
We discard any verification CoT whose parsed labels are inconsistent
with the targets (e.g., $`y`$ or $`z_{1:T}`$), corresponding to the
*consensus filtering* in
[Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").
The training sets of gORM/gPRM contain 34,286/35,666 and 171,780/94,156
verification CoTs for the math and multi-domain settings. See
[Appendices D](#A4 "Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[21](#A5.F21 "Fig. 21 ‣ Appendix E Training Examples ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [22](#A5.F22 "Fig. 22 ‣ Appendix E Training Examples ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
for more details and examples.

### 3.2 Experimental Results

Figure 3: Outcome verification results on ProcessBench in the math
domain.

Figure 4: Best-of-$`N`$ results using
[Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct)
on GSM8K and Math in the math domain.

#### Math-domain results.

First, we evaluate the four verifier variants in the math domain. We
compare outcome-verification performance with a 0.5 decision threshold,
i.e., $`\hat{y}\coloneqq\mathbbm{1}(\hat{f}(x)>0.5)`$.
[Fig. 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
reports F1 score (%) on ProcessBench splits. dPRM outperforms dORM
overall, consistent with prior findings ([Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31)), and shows a slight drop in Omni-Math/OlympiadBench
with 7B backbones. For gORM/gPRM, the overall performance improves with
$`M`$. At small $`M`$, gPRM may lag behind discriminative models (e.g.,
OlympiadBench). gORM generally outperforms gPRM (except 7B-GSM8K), and
the gap widens on Omni-Math/OlympiadBench.

Figure 5: Outcome verification results on MMLU-Pro in the multi-domain
setting.

(a) MMLU-Pro

(b) GPQA-diamond

(c) MedQA and LEXam

Figure 6: Best-of-$`N`$ results using different $`p_{\mathtt{LLM}}`$ on
MMLU-Pro, GPQA-diamond, MedQA, and LEXam.

Although TTS has been well studied in the math domain, evaluations are
not fully controlled: (i) models are rarely compared with a shared
backbone, and (ii) gORM and gPRM have not been directly compared. We
therefore evaluate the reward models with Bo$`N`$ under controlled
conditions. As shown in
[Fig. 4](#S3.F4 "In 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
and consistent with the findings of [Lightman et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib31), dPRM outperforms dORM. Notably, dORM even
underperforms majority voting (MV) with 1.5B backbones, demonstrating
the limitations of coarse outcome-level supervision in the math domain.
In line with [Zhang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib59) and [Khalifa et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib27), generative models outperform discriminative ones,
with gORM slightly surpassing gPRM.

#### Multi-domain and specialized-domain results.

Next, we compare the four variants in the multi-domain setting.
[Fig. 5](#S3.F5 "In Math-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
reports F1 scores (%) for outcome-verification, with a 0.5 decision
threshold, using
[R1-Distill-Qwen-14B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B)
as the reward model backbone. dO/dP/gO/gP denote dORM/dPRM/gORM/gPRM. In
contrast to the math domain results in
[Fig. 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
ORM variants achieve higher F1 scores than PRM variants.

[Fig. 6(a)](#S3.F6.sf1 "In Fig. 6 ‣ Math-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
shows the overall Bo$`N`$ performance using five different
$`p_{\mathtt{LLM}}`$ and
[R1-Distill-Qwen-14B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B)
as the reward model backbone. In this setting, dORM *performs
comparably* to dPRM, while gPRM *lags behind the other variants*, which
is contrary to [Lightman et al. (2024)](#bib.bib31); [Khalifa et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib27) and our math-domain results in
[Fig. 4](#S3.F4 "In 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").
Overall, gORM outperforms dORM/dPRM/gPRM, without notable degradation in
any domain relative to the others (see
[Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F Detailed Results on MMLU-Pro ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
for detailed per-domain results). The same pattern holds for a smaller
backbone
([DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B);
[Fig. 25](#A6.F25 "In Appendix F Detailed Results on MMLU-Pro ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"))
and a non-distilled backbone
([Qwen3-8B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B);
[Fig. 37](#A7.F37 "In Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).
[Table 3](#A7.T3 "In Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
also shows that this trend is not due to insufficient hyperparameter
tuning: sweeping the learning rate and LoRA rank yields only marginal
changes in PRM performance.

To verify that the above observations generalize across datasets, we
take the reward models trained on the MMLU-Pro training split and
evaluate them on GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, and LEXam by generating $`N{=}16`$
CoTs for each question. For MedQA and LEXam, we include only
[SmolLM3-3B](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B) and
[gemma-2-9b-it](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-2-9b-it), since the
other $`p_{\mathtt{LLM}}`$ exhibit severe degradation, even compared to
random guessing. As shown in
[Fig. 6(b)](#S3.F6.sf2 "In Fig. 6 ‣ Math-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
gORM outperforms dORM/dPRM/gPRM on GPQA-Diamond, consistent with the
results on MMLU-Pro
([Fig. 6(a)](#S3.F6.sf1 "In Fig. 6 ‣ Math-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).
In specialized domains
([Fig. 6(c)](#S3.F6.sf3 "In Fig. 6 ‣ Math-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
generative variants significantly outperform discriminative variants and
gORM outperforms gPRM on CoTs generated by
[SmolLM3-3B](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B) and
performs comparably on CoTs generated by
[gemma-2-9b-it](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-2-9b-it).

Figure 7: Best-of-$`N`$ performance gap between all-domain and
single-domain training on MMLU-pro.

#### Effect of multi-domain training.

To assess the effect of multi-domain training, we train and evaluate all
four reward model variants *only* on each MMLU-Pro domain and compare
each variant to its multi-domain counterpart.
[Fig. 7](#S3.F7 "In Multi-domain and specialized-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
shows the degradation in Bo$`N`$ performance with $`N{=}16`$ under
domain-specialized training. We observe *large drops* for dORM and dPRM
under single-domain training relative to their multi-domain
counterparts, with a slightly larger decline for dORM, likely because
outcome-only supervision is sparser than step-level supervision and both
discriminative variants require substantial training data.

In contrast, gORM and gPRM appear more *sample-efficient*: even without
multi-domain training, their performance decreases only modestly (or in
some cases improves). This also explains the results on MedQA and LEXam
([Fig. 6(c)](#S3.F6.sf3 "In Fig. 6 ‣ Math-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")):
the generative variants show strong gains over the discriminative
variants in these sample-inefficient specialized domains (medical and
legal). We defer complete results of single-domain training for the four
reward models to
[Figs. 35](#A6.F35 "In Appendix F Detailed Results on MMLU-Pro ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [36](#A6.F36 "Fig. 36 ‣ Appendix F Detailed Results on MMLU-Pro ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
in
[Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F Detailed Results on MMLU-Pro ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").

## 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings

In this section, we analyze the failure modes of PRMs observed in the
multi-domain setting of
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").

### 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length

(a) Outcome-verification results on “aha” CoTs.

(b) Results on randomly shuffled “aha” CoTs.

Figure 8: (a): ORMs outperform PRMs on “aha” CoTs; however, (b): their
performance drops when intermediate steps are randomly shuffled. This
suggests that ORMs do not simply memorize question-answer pairs.

#### “Aha” CoTs.

As noted in
[Section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
PRMs typically assume that once a reasoning step is incorrect, *all
subsequent steps are incorrect*. However, recent reasoning models can
recover from earlier mistakes and still arrive at the correct answer
([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib20), an “aha” moment;). In such cases, PRMs
can miss the recovery due to a monotonicity bias induced by their
training data. To demonstrate this, we evaluate on “aha” CoTs from
[ProcessBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Qwen/ProcessBench)³³ 3
The “aha” experiments are conducted only on
[ProcessBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Qwen/ProcessBench), which
provides human-annotated step-level labels. For MMLU-Pro, LLM-annotated
process labels would make the rate of “aha” CoTs depend on annotator
reliability. that contain at least one incorrect step
($`\exists\,t\in\{1\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}\ldots\mathord{\mathchar 59\relax}T\}:z_{t}=0`$)
but a correct outcome ($`y=1`$). Overall, “aha” CoTs account for 15.3%
of the cases. In
[Fig. 8(a)](#S4.F8.sf1 "In Fig. 8 ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
we report F1 scores (%) for the “aha” CoTs using $`M{=}16`$ for
gORM/gPRM. We observe that PRM variants perform particularly poorly on
“aha” CoTs. Moreover, scaling the backbone from
[1.5B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B)
to [7B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B)
improves ORM performance, whereas PRM performance degrades with larger
backbones, possibly because larger PRMs are more likely to follow the
PRM assumption inherent in their training data and objective (cf.
[Eqs. 3](#S2.E3 "In Discriminative process reward model (dPRM). ‣ 2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [7](#S2.E7 "Eq. 7 ‣ Generative Process Reward Model (gPRM). ‣ 2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).

#### Do ORMs overfit on “aha” CoTs?

A natural concern about ORM results on “aha” CoTs in
[Fig. 8(a)](#S4.F8.sf1 "In Fig. 8 ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
is *overfitting*: ORMs might only memorize questions and their answers,
thereby correctly verifying “aha” CoTs without checking the correctness
of intermediate reasoning steps. This memorization issue in the math
domain has recently been studied by [Wu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib52). To
investigate this, we conduct the following test: (i) replace the
intermediate reasoning steps $`r_{1:T-1}`$ with $`r^{\prime}_{1:T-1}`$
taken from other CoTs, and (ii) evaluate ORMs on these perturbed CoTs.
If ORMs only memorize the answer in the final reasoning step $`r_{T}`$,
their performance should remain largely unaffected. However,
[Fig. 8(b)](#S4.F8.sf2 "In Fig. 8 ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
shows a significant drop for ORMs (dashed), indicating the reliance on
intermediate steps. Interestingly, the degradation is greater with the
[7B
backbone](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B)
than with the [1.5B
backbone](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B)
for both dORM and gORM. This suggests that larger models rely *more
heavily* on intermediate reasoning steps during verification.

(a) Length distribution of “aha” CoTs.

(b) MV vs. CoT length on MMLU-Pro.

Figure 9: (a): “Aha” moments lengthen CoTs, an effect pronounced in the
multi-domain setting (MMLU-Pro); and (b): majority voting results
degrade significantly with increasing CoT length.

#### Risk increases with CoT length.

“Aha” moments can also lengthen CoTs, an effect especially pronounced in
the multi-domain setting
([Fig. 9(a)](#S4.F9.sf1 "In Fig. 9 ‣ Do ORMs overfit on “aha” CoTs? ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
where LLMs struggle more than in the math domain. As shown in
[Fig. 9(b)](#S4.F9.sf2 "In Fig. 9 ‣ Do ORMs overfit on “aha” CoTs? ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
majority voting results degrade significantly with increasing CoT length
in the multi-domain setting. Consistent with the outcome-verification
failures of PRMs on “aha” CoTs, we argue that *the error of PRM variants
grows with CoT length* ($`T`$). Intuitively, as a CoT grows longer, the
chance that a PRM misclassifies at least one intermediate step rises,
making it more likely to *prematurely* conclude the CoT is incorrect.
Longer CoTs also create more opportunities for “aha” recoveries that
PRMs systematically miss. We formalize this as follows:

###### Theorem 4.1 (Informal: Log-error bound of dORM and gORM; [Theorem A.1](#A1.Thmthm1 "Theorem A.1 (Log-error bound of dORM or gORM). ‣ Assumptions. ‣ A.1 Analysis on Log-Error Bound ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).

Under mild assumptions on the variance of the reward model’s error, the
expected squared log-error of dORM and gORM is bounded by a constant
that is independent of the CoT length $`T`$.

###### Theorem 4.2 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of dPRM; [Theorem A.2](#A1.Thmthm2 "Theorem A.2 (Log-error lower bound of dPRM). ‣ Assumptions. ‣ A.1 Analysis on Log-Error Bound ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).

Assuming a minimum average per-step error variance and bounded local
error correlation, the expected squared log-error of dPRM grows at least
linearly with the CoT length $`T`$.

###### Theorem 4.3 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of sampled gPRM; [Theorem A.3](#A1.Thmthm3 "Theorem A.3 (Log-error lower bound of gPRM). ‣ Assumptions. ‣ A.1 Analysis on Log-Error Bound ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).

Under the same assumptions as
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmthm2 "Theorem 4.2 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of dPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
the expected squared log-error of gPRM also grows at least linearly with
$`T`$. Furthermore, the generative sampling process introduces
additional per-step variance, which strictly worsens this lower bound
compared to dPRM.

All formal definitions, assumptions, and proofs are deferred to
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").
[Theorem 4.1](#S4.Thmthm1 "Theorem 4.1 (Informal: Log-error bound of dORM and gORM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[4.2](#S4.Thmthm2 "Theorem 4.2 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of dPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [4.3](#S4.Thmthm3 "Theorem 4.3 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of sampled gPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
establish that while dORM/gORM error bounds remain stable regardless of
length, dPRM/gPRM lower bounds grow linearly with $`T`$. In
[Theorem A.4](#A1.Thmthm4 "Theorem A.4 (Log-error lower bound of mean-gPRM). ‣ Jensen-gap representation (mean predictor). ‣ A.1 Analysis on Log-Error Bound ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
we additionally show that for gPRM with Monte Carlo estimation (cf.
[Eq. 8](#S2.E8 "In Generative Process Reward Model (gPRM). ‣ 2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
the log-error lower bound also increases linearly with $`T`$.

Figure 10: (Left): Outcome verification vs. CoT length; (Right): TTS
improvement vs. average CoT length.

#### Empirical support.

To empirically support
[Theorem 4.1](#S4.Thmthm1 "Theorem 4.1 (Informal: Log-error bound of dORM and gORM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[4.2](#S4.Thmthm2 "Theorem 4.2 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of dPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [4.3](#S4.Thmthm3 "Theorem 4.3 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of sampled gPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
we plot the F1 score (%) for outcome-verification in the multi-domain
setting as a function of the number of CoT steps ($`T`$) in
[Fig. 10](#S4.F10 "In Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")-(Left).
We divide CoTs into eight bins: 1-2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7-8, 9-13, and 14-162
steps. As $`T`$ increases, dPRM/gPRM degrade considerably relative to
dORM/gORM.
[Fig. 10](#S4.F10 "In Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")-(Right)
shows the performance improvements over majority voting for different
categories with respect to the average number of CoT steps. We observe
negative correlations for dPRM (-0.058) and gPRM (-0.608), while dORM
(0.316) and gORM (0.399) show positive correlations. These results not
only provide empirical support for
[Theorem 4.1](#S4.Thmthm1 "Theorem 4.1 (Informal: Log-error bound of dORM and gORM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[4.2](#S4.Thmthm2 "Theorem 4.2 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of dPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [4.3](#S4.Thmthm3 "Theorem 4.3 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of sampled gPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
but also demonstrate that increasing CoT length can degrade TTS
performance for dPRM and gPRM in the multi-domain setting.

### 4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs

![Refer to caption](2510.00492v3/colorbar_1p5b.png)

![Refer to caption](2510.00492v3/colorbar_7b.png)

Figure 11: Outcome-verification results of PRMs vs. label noise on
GSM8K.

#### Label noise risk.

Beyond CoT-length effects, *label noise* poses an additional risk,
especially in multi-domain settings. Since human annotation of long CoTs
is more costly in specialized domains such as law and medicine than in
math, prior work often relies on LLMs to automatically label process
steps ([Zeng et al., 2025](#bib.bib58)), which introduces noise that can
degrade PRM performance. Indeed, recent evaluations in the math domain
document that automated annotation pipelines, such as Monte Carlo
estimation, can inject substantial label noise and evaluation
artifacts ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib60)). We study this by
injecting synthetic noise into the process labels of PRM800K. We vary
the level of noise along two axes: (i) *process-noise ratio* (the
per-step probability of flipping a process label) and (ii) *data-noise
ratio* (the fraction of examples to which noise is applied). We report
the outcome-verification F1 score (%) in
[Fig. 11](#S4.F11 "In 4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
for
[1.5B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B)
and [7B](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B)
backbones, using greedy decoding for generative variants. dPRM is highly
sensitive to label noise, demonstrating its potential vulnerability in
multi-domain settings. In contrast, gPRM is more robust, which is
consistent with reports that LLM memorization can make random label
noise act as a regularizer in math ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)).

#### Length shift hurts gPRM.

We further analyze why gPRM degrades in the multi-domain setting,
despite its robustness to label noise in math. As CoTs become longer,
the imperfect $`p_{\texttt{LLM-j}}`$ struggles to align stepwise
verification rationales with process labels. As a result, *consensus
filtering* prunes long CoTs, shifting the training CoT-length
distribution away from the test set
([Fig. 12](#S4.F12 "In Length shift hurts gPRM. ‣ 4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).

We quantify the above length distribution shift with the Wasserstein
distance ([Kantorovich, 1960](#bib.bib25)), reporting distances from the
test set to the unfiltered pool (Train), the gORM training set, and the
gPRM training set. In the math domain
([Table 4](#A7.T4 "In Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
gPRM has the smallest distance (e.g., overall: 2.760/2.430/1.600 for
Train/gORM/gPRM), whereas in the multi-domain setting
([Figs. 12](#S4.F12 "In Length shift hurts gPRM. ‣ 4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [5](#A7.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"))
it has the largest distance (e.g., overall: 0.202/0.532/3.083 for
Train/gORM/gPRM).

Figure 12: Length distribution shift on MMLU-Pro (overall/per-domain)
measured by Wasserstein distance.

Figure 13: Per-domain Bo$`N`$ improvement over majority voting vs.
Wasserstein distance on MMLU-Pro.

The distribution shift of gPRM also corresponds to its degradation
across domains, observed in the multi-domain setting
([Fig. 6(a)](#S3.F6.sf1 "In Fig. 6 ‣ Math-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).
[Fig. 13](#S4.F13 "In Length shift hurts gPRM. ‣ 4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
shows a strong negative correlation between the Wasserstein distance and
per-domain improvement over majority voting with $`N{=}16`$ for gPRM
($`-0.625`$), whereas correlations are weak for the other methods
($`0.345/0.048/0.082`$ for dORM/dPRM/gORM). Together, these results
suggest that *consensus filtering* induces a length-distribution shift
that disproportionately affects gPRM in the multi-domain setting,
despite its robustness to label noise.

#### Label refinement and relaxed filtering.

To mitigate the CoT-length distribution shift for gPRM, we further test
label refinement with [Gemini-2.0
Flash](https://blog.google/technology/google-deepmind/google-gemini-ai-update-december-2024/) ([Comanici
et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)) and relaxed consensus filtering. Although both
increase the CoT survival rate, they neither substantially reduce the
Wasserstein distance nor improve downstream performance. See
[Tables 5](#A7.T5 "In Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
[6](#A7.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [7](#A7.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
in
[Appendix G](#A7 "Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
for more details.

## 5 Practical Guidelines, Limitations, and Future Work

This section suggests practical guidance, clarifies limitations, and
outlines future directions. Building on the empirical and theoretical
results of
[Sections 3](#S3 "3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [4](#S4 "4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
we summarize when each reward-model variant is preferable in the table
below, and then connect the entries to the supporting evidence.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| (i) | *Short* CoTs, *clean* labels, *tight* latency | dPRM |
| \[1pt/1pt\] (ii) | *Long* CoTs / *frequent error recoveries* | gORM if compute permits; else dORM |
| \[1pt/1pt\] (iii) | *Mixed/shifting domains* | gORM |
| \[1pt/1pt\] (iv) | *High label noise* |     ORM  PRMs amplify early errors |
| \[1pt/1pt\] (v) | *Strict compute/latency* |     dORM/dPRM  gORM and gPRM add sampling overhead |
| \[1pt/1pt\] (vi) | *Limited training data* |     gORM/gPRM  Higher sample efficiency |

#### From findings to recommendations.

Rows (i) and (ii) follow from our CoT-length analysis in
[Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").
When CoTs are short and process labels are clean, the per-step signal
exploited by dPRM is informative and its discriminative head keeps
inference cheap, matching the math-domain regime where dPRM is
competitive
([Fig. 4](#S3.F4 "In 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).
As $`T`$ grows, however,
[Theorem 4.2](#S4.Thmthm2 "Theorem 4.2 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of dPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [4.3](#S4.Thmthm3 "Theorem 4.3 (Informal: Log-error lower bound of sampled gPRM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
show that the log-error lower bounds of dPRM and gPRM grow linearly with
$`T`$, while
[Theorem 4.1](#S4.Thmthm1 "Theorem 4.1 (Informal: Log-error bound of dORM and gORM; ). ‣ Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
bounds the ORM error independently of $`T`$. This is corroborated in
[Fig. 10](#S4.F10 "In Risk increases with CoT length. ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
(length-vs-improvement correlations of $`-0.058`$/$`-0.608`$ for
dPRM/gPRM versus $`0.316`$/$`0.399`$ for dORM/gORM) and by the “aha”
analysis in
[Fig. 8(a)](#S4.F8.sf1 "In Fig. 8 ‣ 4.1 Risk of PRMs with CoT Length ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
where PRMs systematically miss recoveries from earlier mistakes, hence
the ORM recommendation in row (ii).

Rows (iii)-(vi) reflect the multi-domain and resource trade-offs
surfaced in
[Sections 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [3](#S3 "3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling").
For mixed or shifting domains, *consensus filtering* prunes long CoTs
and induces a length-distribution shift that disproportionately hurts
gPRM (largest Wasserstein distance in
[Table 5](#A7.T5 "In Appendix G Additional Analysis ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"),
with a correlation of $`-0.625`$ between distance and per-domain
improvement in
[Fig. 13](#S4.F13 "In Length shift hurts gPRM. ‣ 4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
motivating gORM as the default. Under high label noise, the PRM800K
noise-injection study
([Fig. 11](#S4.F11 "In 4.2 Label Noise and Consensus Filtering of PRMs ‣ 4 Analysis on Why PRMs Fail in the Multi-Domain Settings ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling"))
shows that dPRM is highly sensitive to per-step label flips and that
even the more robust gPRM inherits the monotonicity assumption that
amplifies early errors, so ORMs are the safer choice.

Finally, gORM/gPRM are slower than discriminative variants because they
autoregressively generate verification tokens with $`M`$ rollouts (cf.
[Eq. 8](#S2.E8 "In Generative Process Reward Model (gPRM). ‣ 2.2 Reward Models ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
while dORM/dPRM score each CoT in a single forward pass. On MMLU-Pro
with CoTs from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the normalized inference times are
0.0005/0.0005/0.0571/0.0306 seconds per CoT for dORM/dPRM/gORM/gPRM,
respectively, making dORM/dPRM preferable under strict compute or
latency budgets. Although gPRM is $`1.87\times`$ faster than gORM due to
early stopping, it may miss “aha” CoTs; thus, we recommend gORM when
reliability is prioritized, especially in medical and legal domains. In
contrast, generative variants better exploit LLM priors and
rationale-style supervision, improving sample efficiency with limited
training data
([Fig. 7](#S3.F7 "In Multi-domain and specialized-domain results. ‣ 3.2 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and
[Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F Detailed Results on MMLU-Pro ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")),
so we recommend them in row (vi).

#### Limitations and future work.

While we present a thorough analysis of four reward model variants, our
study has several limitations: (i) All models are trained via supervised
fine–tuning. One could instead use a generative verifier to roll out
rationales and treat agreement between their verdict and the GT label as
a reward signal for reinforcement learning (RL). Because using RL to
train verifiers/reward models is uncommon and introduces additional
confounders, we exclude RL-based training from our analysis. (ii) Owing
to computational constraints, we adopt LoRA adapters rather than
full-parameter fine-tuning. This choice may affect performance and
scaling behavior. However, we expect the qualitative trends to hold.
(iii) Following most of the PRM literature ([Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31); [Zeng et al., 2025](#bib.bib58)), we do not consider
tool use, however, [Gou et al. (2024)](#bib.bib17) showed that tool use
can help reduce auto-label noise. In future work, we plan to extend our
analysis to broader task domains, model families, and training regimes.
We also plan to explicitly study tool-augmented verification and
inference pipelines.

## Broader Impact Statement

This work evaluates verification strategies for test-time scaling of
LLMs across multiple domains. It does not involve human subjects, user
studies, or the collection of personally identifiable information. All
datasets used are publicly available benchmarks and were accessed under
their respective licenses. To the best of our knowledge, they do not
contain sensitive personal data.

A natural direction for future work is to increase the trustworthiness
of LLM outputs in real systems by verifying them, thereby reducing
reasoning errors and hallucinations. Although our experiments include
legal and medical-themed datasets (e.g., law and health), the models and
methods are research artifacts and are not intended for real-world
legal, medical, or other high-stakes decision-making. They should not
substitute professional judgment, and any deployment in such settings
would require additional domain-specific validation, safety auditing,
and regulatory compliance.

## Reproducibility Statement

We believe that we provide sufficient materials, including prompts,
hyperparameters, model backbones, training details, and the synthetic
data generation process, throughout the main paper
([Sections 2](#S2 "2 Background and Related Work ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")
and [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling")).
````
